# Loop Engineering: A Guide for Engineers and Practitioners

## How to design, verify, and govern agentic AI loops in production: triggers, topologies, failure modes, cost control, and observability.

[![Adnan Masood, PhD.](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/1*Ua7jPEgql2zYNV9JFl2HLA.jpeg)](/@adnanmasood?source=post_page---byline--893bb65ea943---------------------------------------)[Adnan Masood, PhD.](/@adnanmasood?source=post_page---byline--893bb65ea943---------------------------------------)Follow35 min read23 hours ago3

[Listen](/plans?dimension=post_audio_button&postId=893bb65ea943&source=upgrade_membership---post_audio_button-----------------------------------------)Share

More

> tl;dr — The goal post of hard engineering problems in agentic AI have moved. Prompt phrasing stopped being the bottleneck somewhere in early 2026, and what replaced it is loop design: the trigger, the topology, the verifier, and the stop rules that decide what an agent does next and when it quits. Loop engineering got its name in June 2026, the week Addy Osmani published the essay and Peter Steinberger compressed it into a sentence: stop prompting your agents and start designing the loops that prompt them. Boris Cherny, who built Claude Code, said the same from the vendor side, that his job now is to write the loops that drive Claude. The phrase caught on because it named a wall every team running agents in production had already hit. A good prompt fixes one turn. It says nothing about which turn comes next, what counts as done, who signs off before an irreversible action, or how spend stays capped. Those are loop questions, and the answers are what decide whether an agentic system survives contact with a real workload. This guide is my working map of that territory, written for engineers putting agents into production.

Press enter or click to view image in full size![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*pMCTca1XYHt4urUW4FEteg.png)Loop engineering is the discipline of designing the control system that prompts, evaluates, routes, and stops an agent, in place of prompting the agent by hand one turn at a time. The field crystallized as a named practice in June 2026, after several months of adjacent work on context engineering and harness engineering, because production teams kept discovering that the hard problems had moved. The phrasing of a prompt stopped being the bottleneck. Trigger choice, topology, context hygiene, verification, stop rules, observability, governance, and budget control became the bottleneck. The lesson I keep returning to is blunt. The agent is one component.

The loop is the production system. Teams that treat the model as the whole system inherit drift, runaway cost, unverifiable output, and brittle autonomy. Teams that engineer the loop as a bounded control plane ship long-running agentic systems with tractable failure modes, measurable economics, and auditable behavior [1]-[4], [9]-[11], [17]-[18].

Press enter or click to view image in full size![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*6Fx8cVMgjIWaI5we3aJh2g.png)### Some Terminology

A **prompt** is a single, stateless request to a model. A **harness** is the runtime environment around an agent: tools, memory, permissions, prompts, models, and instrumentation [1]. A **workflow** is a predetermined execution graph whose edges are selected by code. A **loop** is a stateful control cycle that repeatedly observes, reasons, acts, verifies, and then decides whether to continue. Loop engineering begins exactly where automation stops being sufficient, at the point where the runtime must repeatedly choose its next move from fresh observations and explicit policy [1], [18].

## Part I. The Discipline and Its Lineage

Press enter or click to view image in full size![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*RK2mlXCVN2jmxZFXJkJkoA.png)The path into loop engineering is visible in the public writing of early 2026, and it reads as four datable phases.

Phase one was prompt engineering. We optimized the lexical structure of a single query to raise the quality of an isolated response. Phase two was context engineering. We added retrieval and context-window management to control what the model evaluated during inference. Phase three was harness engineering. In February 2026 Mitchell Hashimoto, the creator of Terraform and Ghostty, published an essay describing a habit he had formed while working with agents: every time an agent made a mistake, he engineered a permanent fix into the agent’s environment so the failure became structurally impossible to repeat. He called it engineering the harness, and he framed tool contracts, context loading, action boundaries, and execution environment as first-class engineering surfaces [1].

Phase four is loop engineering, and it stabilized in the second week of June 2026. Addy Osmani published an essay on June 7 that named the next layer explicitly and defined it as replacing yourself, the person who prompts the agent, with a system that does the prompting for you [2]. The same day, Peter Steinberger compressed the idea into the sentence that triggered the naming event: stop prompting coding agents, and design the loops that prompt your agents instead [3]. Secondary reporting on June 11 measured that originating post at roughly 2.2 million views [5]. I treat that figure as indicative rather than audited, since it is a single secondary source counting a single platform.

What moved this from slogan to architecture was the vendor side. Boris Cherny, one of the principal builders behind Claude Code, stated publicly in early June that he no longer prompts Claude. He writes loops that prompt Claude and decide what it does next [4]. That matters because the product surface had already converged on the same reality. The `/goal` command, scheduled routines, subagents, hooks, agent teams, and built-in tracing are loop primitives. They are not chat affordances [9]-[10].

The reason the discipline emerged in mid-2026 is operational, and I want to be precise about it. Prompt engineering improved single turns. Context engineering improved what each turn knew. Harness engineering improved the runtime around a turn. Production teams then hit the same missing layer over and over: who decides the next turn, what fresh evidence is required before proceeding, which tools are reachable, how long the system runs, what “done” means, who approves an irreversible action, and how spend is capped. Those are loop questions, and the major frameworks now answer them as such. Anthropic documents the agent loop as a first-class subsystem of the Claude Agent SDK. OpenAI’s Agents SDK exposes traces, spans, handoffs, guardrails, and usage across a run. LangGraph draws an explicit line between workflows with predetermined paths and agents that define their own process dynamically [17]-[18].

The leverage argument is simple, and it is the whole reason to care. A prompt improves one run. A loop improves every run that follows until the runtime or the policy changes. That places loop engineering with platform engineering and distributed systems, well away from hand-authored prompting. The durable artifacts are termination logic, verifier design, trace schemas, tool permissioning, checkpoint storage, and budget policy. Those artifacts survive a model swap. Hand-authored prompts usually do not.

## Part II. Anatomy of the Agent Loop

Press enter or click to view image in full size![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*zSOgsS3VPnIZZ_fKGZmBuQ.png)The historical substrate beneath every production loop is the interleaved reasoning-and-action pattern that builders trace back to ReAct, developed at Princeton and Google [6]. In production terms the canonical cycle is perceive, reason, plan, act, observe, and then decide whether to continue. The reason this pattern became a systems discipline in 2026 is that vendors stopped exposing it only as paper logic and started shipping it as long-running, tool-using, self-checking loops [9], [17]-[18].

A production loop has six minimal elements. It needs a goal representation, a trigger, a state store, a policy for selecting the next action, a verifier, and a stop rule. I use this decomposition as a diagnostic. Remove the verifier and you get self-affirming autonomy. Remove the stop rule and you get unbounded spend. Remove state and the loop repeats work or drifts. Remove the trigger and the loop never starts or never resumes. Every current vendor surface maps onto these six elements. Anthropic exposes hooks, stop hooks, routines, cost controls, memory, and subagents. OpenAI exposes `/goal`, handoffs, traces, spans, and guardrails. LangGraph exposes the graph runtime, thread state, checkpoints, and the workflow-versus-agent distinction [9]-[11], [17]-[18].

Osmani’s practitioner enumeration overlaps this control view and is worth keeping alongside it. He describes automations as scheduled triggers that begin discovery and triage without a human, worktrees as isolated environments that keep parallel subagents from corrupting shared state, skills as codified project knowledge that replaces hallucination with explicit domain rules, plugins and connectors as the interfaces to external infrastructure, and subagents as specialized roles that establish a maker-checker dynamic, with a persistent state store such as a Markdown file or an issue board that records completed and pending work outside the context window [2]. Read his five building blocks as the engineer’s parts list and read the six control elements as the systems contract they must satisfy.

The boundary between a loop and a deterministic automation comes down to one question: who selects the next edge. In an automation, code selects edges from predefined conditions, and the program fails on the first unhandled exception. In a loop, the runtime repeatedly asks the model or a planner to choose among actions based on new observations, while policy and governance constrain that choice. LangGraph states this plainly in its own documentation, distinguishing workflows with predetermined code paths from agents that define their own process and tool use [18]. The consequence for testing is direct. Workflow tests target graph edges. Loop tests target trajectory properties and policy compliance across many possible edges.

The Ralph lineage made loop behavior legible to practitioners before the term stabilized. Geoffrey Huntley’s Ralph Wiggum loop circulated through 2025 as a recognizable pattern: feed an identical prompt file to an agent in a simple shell loop, intercept the model’s attempts to exit using a stop hook, and force the agent to read its own prior work off the filesystem and iterate on its failures [7]. The academic follow-up, “Supervising Ralph Wiggum” by Xu, Martelaro, and McComb, formalized a lesson production teams now treat as table stakes. Baseline agents fixate on existing paradigms and fail to explore alternatives. A metacognitive co-regulation loop, which deploys a second agent to supervise the primary worker’s metacognition, navigates the design space better than the bare Ralph loop and produces stronger results [8]. The engineering takeaway is the one I enforce in every review. Keep the stop authority outside the worker model whenever the action is costly or irreversible.

## Part III. Loop Topologies and Trigger Models

Press enter or click to view image in full size![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*7rY0tt3e5fzCeA-5Rp8qlA.png)Trigger design determines both the cost profile and the escalation profile of a loop, so I treat it as the first decision, ahead of model and topology. Four trigger classes matter in 2026: cron, heartbeat, hook, and goal. Cron and heartbeat are scheduled wakes. Hooks are event-bound interceptors attached to runtime lifecycle points. Goal triggers are semantic persistence primitives that keep the system working until a condition holds. Anthropic documents `/goal` as a built-in shortcut for a session-scoped, prompt-based Stop hook, and it documents routines for scheduled execution and hooks for tool and lifecycle events [9]. OpenAI documents `/goal` as a persistent goal mode available in the app, the IDE extension, and the CLI [14]-[15].
